lessons.title: Release profiles
lessons.objective_md: Tell the dev and release profiles apart, and change a profile's settings in `Cargo.toml`.

screens.heading: Two ways to build
screens.text_md:
Cargo builds with a **profile**: a named set of settings for the compiler. Two are built in. `cargo build` uses **dev**, tuned for fast builds while you work: little optimisation, plenty of debug information. `cargo build --release` uses **release**, tuned for the program you ship: slower to build, faster to run.

The two builds go to different folders, `target/debug/` and `target/release/`, so one never overwrites the other. Both print `500000500000`; the release one gets there sooner.

coming_from.c: Like `-O0 -g` versus `-O3`: Cargo names the two sets of flags `dev` and `release` and keeps their outputs apart.
coming_from.go: `go build` has one mode; Rust separates a quick dev build from an optimised release build.
coming_from.java: Like Debug and Release configurations in Visual Studio or Maven profiles: the same code, built with different settings.
coming_from.js: Like a bundler's development and production modes: one builds fast and is easy to debug, the other is optimised for users.
coming_from.python: There's no compile step in Python to tune. Cargo's profiles are like choosing between running your code under a debugger and shipping an optimised build.

panels.title: $ cargo build
panels.text:
Compiling sums v0.1.0
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s)
   Compiling sums v0.1.0
    Finished `release` profile [optimized] target(s)

screens.heading: The defaults
screens.text_md:
Each profile has defaults, and you only write the settings you want to change. The one you'll meet most is **`opt-level`**, how hard the compiler optimises, from `0` (not at all) to `3` (as much as it can).

These two tables restate the defaults, so adding them changes nothing. Profiles have other settings too, such as whether integer overflow is checked: on in dev, off in release, where overflow wraps around silently instead of panicking.

code.text:
[profile.dev]
opt-level = 0

[profile.release]
opt-level = 3

question.prompt_md: Which command builds with the release profile?

explanations.text_md: Correct. `--release` selects the release profile; the result goes to `target/release/`.
Not quite. Plain `cargo build` uses the dev profile.
Not quite. There's no `--debug` flag; dev is already the default.
Not quite. Cargo has no `release` subcommand.

screens.heading: Overriding one setting
screens.text_md:
(below the panels)

A `[profile.dev]` table overrides only the keys it lists. `opt-level = 1` makes dev builds a bit slower to compile and their programs noticeably faster, a common choice for games and simulations that are too slow to test unoptimised.

code.text:
[package]
name = "sums"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

right.label: A faster dev build

code.text:
[package]
name = "sums"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[profile.dev]
opt-level = 1

right.caption_md: Dev builds now optimise a little; every other dev setting keeps its default.

screens.heading: Overflow in the two profiles
screens.text_md:
Profiles can change behaviour too, not just speed. In a dev build, `level + 1` on a `u8` holding 255 panics with "attempt to add with overflow". In a release build the check is off and the result wraps around to 0.

Code shouldn't depend on either: when overflow is possible, say what you want. `checked_add` returns `None` on overflow; `wrapping_add` wraps on purpose. This program prints `None` and `0` in both profiles.

question.prompt_md: Adding `[profile.release]` with `opt-level = 3` to `Cargo.toml` makes release builds faster than before.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. `opt-level = 3` is already the release default, so the table changes nothing.
Correct. A profile table only matters for settings that differ from the defaults.

screens.heading: Profiles belong to the workspace root
screens.text_md: When several packages share a workspace (L14.4), they share one build, so profiles are set once, in the **root** `Cargo.toml`, and apply to every member. A `[profile]` table in a member's own manifest is ignored, and Cargo warns about it.

code.text:
[workspace]
members = ["core", "cli"]
resolver = "3"

[profile.dev]
opt-level = 1

screens.heading: Which profile does each command use?
screens.text_md:
| Command | Profile |
|---|---|
| `cargo build`, `cargo run`, `cargo check` | dev |
| `cargo build --release`, `cargo run --release` | release |
| `cargo test` | test, based on dev |
| `cargo bench` | bench, based on release |
| `cargo install` | release |

Tests use dev settings because you run them often and want them to build quickly; `cargo install` uses release because it builds a program for you to use.

question.prompt_md: Fill in the blank so dev builds optimise a little.

code.text:
[profile.dev]
___ = 1

question.general_md: `opt-level` sets how much the compiler optimises, from 0 to 3; dev's default is 0.

wrong_answers.why_md: Cargo's key is `opt-level`.
that's a profile name, not a setting.

summary: `cargo build` uses the **dev** profile; `cargo build --release` uses **release**. They build into `target/debug/` and `target/release/`.
A `[profile.dev]` or `[profile.release]` table overrides only the keys it lists, such as `opt-level` (0 to 3).
Dev checks integer overflow and panics; release wraps. Use `checked_` or `wrapping_` methods when overflow is possible.
In a workspace, profiles go in the root `Cargo.toml`.

lessons.title: Documentation comments and doc tests
lessons.book_section: 14.2 Publishing a Crate to Crates.io (documentation comments)
lessons.objective_md: Write `///` and `//!` documentation in Markdown, with the usual sections, and run its examples as tests.

screens.heading: Comments that become documentation
screens.text_md:
A comment that starts with **three** slashes, `///`, is a **documentation comment**. It documents the item right after it and is written in Markdown: `# Examples` is a heading, and the fenced block is code.

`cargo doc` turns these comments into HTML pages, the same kind you read on docs.rs; `cargo doc --open` builds them and opens them in a browser. Ordinary `//` comments are for people reading the code and never appear there.

coming_from.c: Like Doxygen comments, with the generator built into Cargo and examples that are compiled and run.
coming_from.go: Like Go doc comments above declarations, and like `Example` functions, the code samples are tested.
coming_from.java: Like Javadoc or XML doc comments: `cargo doc` plays the role of the `javadoc` tool.
coming_from.js: Like JSDoc (`/** … */`), but in Markdown instead of `@param` tags, and `cargo doc` is built in.
coming_from.python: Like docstrings, but written above the item with `///`. And like doctest, the examples in them run as tests.

screens.heading: The usual sections
screens.text_md:
Most documented functions use some of these headings:

- **`# Examples`**: how to call it. The most useful section; readers often skip straight to it.
- **`# Panics`**: the situations in which it panics, so callers can avoid them.
- **`# Errors`**: for a function returning `Result`, which errors it can return and when.
- **`# Safety`**: for an `unsafe` function (Chapter 20), what the caller must guarantee.

Leave out sections that don't apply: a function that never panics doesn't need `# Panics`, though saying "never panics" can be useful when readers might wonder.

question.prompt_md: Which comment documents the function `parse` written right below it?

explanations.text_md: Correct. `///` documents the item that follows it, and `cargo doc` shows it on that item's page.
Not quite. `//` is an ordinary comment; it never reaches the documentation.
Not quite. `//!` documents the item that *contains* it, usually the whole crate.
Not quite. A block comment is an ordinary comment too.

screens.heading: Examples are tests
screens.text_md:
`cargo test` also runs the code blocks in your documentation, as **doc tests**. Each block becomes a small program that uses your crate from the outside, which is why it calls `my_crate::add_one` with the crate's name. If the code doesn't compile, or an `assert_eq!` fails, the test fails, so an example can't quietly go out of date.

`cargo test --doc` runs only the doc tests.

panels.title: $ cargo test --doc
panels.text:
Doc-tests my_crate

running 1 test
test src/lib.rs - add_one (line 5) ... ok

test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out

screens.heading: When an example goes wrong
screens.text_md: Here the example claims `add_one(5)` is 7. The function is right and the documentation is wrong, and the doc test catches it: the `assert_eq!` fails, the report names the file, the function and the line where the block starts, and `cargo test` fails.

panels.title: $ cargo test --doc
panels.text:
running 1 test
test src/lib.rs - add_one (line 5) ... FAILED

failures:

---- src/lib.rs - add_one (line 5) stdout ----
Test executable failed (exit status: 101).

stderr:
assertion `left == right` failed
  left: 7
 right: 6

test result: FAILED. 0 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out

question.prompt_md: A doc test calls the crate's functions through the crate's name, as `my_crate::add_one`, because each example is compiled as a separate program that uses the crate.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Doc tests see your crate the way its users do: only the public API, through the crate's name.
Not quite. An example inside the crate can't use private items or `crate::` paths, because it isn't part of the crate.

screens.heading: Documenting the crate itself
screens.text_md: `//!` documents the item that **contains** the comment rather than the one after it. At the top of `src/lib.rs` that's the crate, so these lines become the front page of its documentation: what the crate is for and where to start.

screens.heading: Examples that shouldn't run
screens.text_md:
(below the panels)

`no_run` is for examples that would do something unwanted in a test, such as using the network. `ignore` skips the example entirely, so nothing checks it; reach for it only when the code can't compile on its own, and prefer a runnable example.

left.label: Runs
left.caption_md: A plain fence is compiled and run by `cargo test`.

right.label: Compiled only
right.caption_md: `no_run` checks that the example compiles but doesn't run it.

question.prompt_md: Fill in the blank to run only the documentation examples.

code.text: cargo test ___

question.general_md: `cargo test --doc` runs the doc tests and skips unit and integration tests.

wrong_answers.why_md: the flag is `--doc`.
that builds the programs in an `examples/` folder, not documentation code.

summary: `///` documents the next item and `//!` the containing one (usually the crate), in Markdown.
Common sections: `# Examples`, `# Panics`, `# Errors`, `# Safety`.
`cargo doc` builds HTML documentation; `cargo doc --open` opens it.
Code blocks in documentation are doc tests: `cargo test` compiles and runs them as outside users of the crate. `cargo test --doc` runs only them; `no_run` compiles without running.

lessons.title: A convenient public API, and publishing
lessons.objective_md: Shape a crate's public API with `pub use`, and know what publishing to crates.io involves.

screens.heading: A structure that suits the author
screens.text_md: The Book's `art` crate organises its code into modules that make sense to its author: types in `kinds`, functions in `utils`. A user, though, has to learn that layout to write `use art::kinds::PrimaryColor;` and `use art::utils::mix;`, and the front page of the documentation lists only two modules, hiding the items people came for.

screens.heading: Re-exporting at the root
screens.text_md:
(below the panels)

`pub use` re-exports an item: it becomes part of the crate's public API at a new path, while staying where it is. The old paths still work, and the documentation's front page now lists the re-exported items. The internal layout can change later without breaking users.

coming_from.c: Like a public umbrella header that includes the internal ones, but checked by the compiler and with privacy kept intact.
coming_from.go: Go packages can't re-export; Rust crates can publish a short path to an item defined deeper inside.
coming_from.java: Java has no re-exports; you'd add a facade class. C# `using` aliases don't change what a library exposes. Rust's `pub use` does.
coming_from.js: Like an `index.ts` that does `export { mix } from "./utils"`.
coming_from.python: Like importing names into a package's `__init__.py` so users write `from art import mix`.

left.label: Without re-exports
left.caption_md: Users must know the internal modules.

right.label: With `pub use` in `art`
right.caption_md: `pub use self::kinds::PrimaryColor;` and `pub use self::utils::mix;` in `art`'s `src/lib.rs` make short paths work.

question.prompt_md: `art` has `pub mod utils { pub fn mix(…) … }` and, at its root, `pub use self::utils::mix;`. Which paths can users write?

options.text_md: Neither: re-exports are only for the crate's own code.

explanations.text_md: Correct. The re-export adds a path; the original public path still works, and both name the same function.
Not quite. `utils` is still a public module, so its path stays valid. Make it private to hide it.
Not quite. `pub use` makes `art::mix` public too.
Not quite. The `pub` in `pub use` is exactly what makes the new path available to users.

screens.heading: Setting up to publish
screens.text_md:
Publishing puts your crate on **crates.io** for anyone to depend on. First you create an account there (it uses a GitHub login) and an API token, then run `cargo login` once, which stores the token on your computer. Keep the token secret: anyone who has it can publish as you.

This course never asks you to do any of this; every exercise builds locally.

screens.heading: Metadata
screens.text_md: crates.io needs a few fields before it accepts a crate: a unique `name` (first come, first served), a `description` shown in search results, and a `license`, written as an SPDX identifier such as `MIT` or `MIT OR Apache-2.0` (the one Rust itself uses). `publish = false` in `[package]` does the opposite: it makes `cargo publish` refuse, which protects private packages.

code.text:
[package]
name = "guessing_game"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"
description = "A fun game where you guess what number the computer has chosen."
license = "MIT OR Apache-2.0"

[dependencies]

question.prompt_md: Once a version is published to crates.io, you can't overwrite it or delete it.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Publishing is permanent, so every project that depends on that version keeps building. To fix a mistake, publish a new version.
Not quite. You can *yank* a version (next screen), but its code stays available to projects that already use it.

screens.heading: Versions and publishing
screens.text_md:
`cargo publish` packages the crate and uploads it. To release changes, raise `version` in `Cargo.toml` and publish again. Versions follow **semantic versioning**: `1.2.3` → `1.2.4` for a fix, `1.3.0` for new features that don't break anything, `2.0.0` for a breaking change. A `pub use` façade helps here: you can rearrange internal modules in a minor release, because the public paths stay the same.

A version, once published, is permanent.

screens.heading: Yanking a version
screens.text_md:
If a version has a serious bug, **yank** it: `cargo yank --vers 1.0.1`. New projects can no longer pick it, but projects whose `Cargo.lock` already names it still build. `cargo yank --vers 1.0.1 --undo` reverses it.

Yanking deletes no code. If you published a secret by accident, yanking doesn't help: change the secret at once.

question.prompt_md: Version 1.0.1 of your crate has a bug that corrupts data. What should you do?

options.text_md: Publish 1.0.2 with the fix, and yank 1.0.1.
Yank 1.0.1 and nothing else: yanking removes the code.

explanations.text_md: Correct. The fix needs a new version, and yanking stops new projects from choosing the broken one.
Not quite. Published versions can't be deleted.
Not quite. A version number can be published only once.
Not quite. Yanking hides a version from new projects; existing lockfiles still use it, and nobody gets a fix.

summary: `pub use` re-exports an item at a new public path: users get short paths, and the internal layout stays free to change.
Publishing needs a crates.io account, `cargo login`, and `name`, `description` and `license` in `Cargo.toml`.
Published versions are permanent; follow semantic versioning and publish a new version to fix one.
`cargo yank` stops new projects from picking a version without deleting it.

lessons.title: Workspaces
lessons.objective_md: Build several related packages as one workspace, connect them with path dependencies, and build, run and test one member at a time.

screens.heading: A workspace
screens.text_md:
As a project grows, you may split it into several packages: a library and the program that uses it, say. A **workspace** is a set of packages that share one `Cargo.lock` and one `target/` folder, so they're built together and agree on dependency versions.

The root `Cargo.toml` above has no `[package]`: it's a **virtual manifest** that only lists the **members**, each a folder with its own `Cargo.toml`. `resolver = "3"` picks the current dependency resolver, which a virtual manifest has to name because it has no edition.

code.text:
[workspace]
members = ["adder", "add_one"]
resolver = "3"

coming_from.c: Like a top-level CMake project with several subdirectory targets, but with dependencies declared per package.
coming_from.go: Like a Go workspace (`go.work`) listing several modules.
coming_from.java: Like a multi-module Maven or Gradle build, or a .NET solution with several projects.
coming_from.js: Like npm or pnpm workspaces: a root `package.json` lists the packages, and they share one lock file and install.
coming_from.python: Like a monorepo of several packages managed together, with one lock file for all of them.

screens.heading: The layout
screens.text_md:
The Book's workspace has a binary package, `adder`, and a library package, `add_one`:

```text
├── Cargo.lock
├── Cargo.toml
├── add_one
│   ├── Cargo.toml
│   └── src
│       └── lib.rs
├── adder
│   ├── Cargo.toml
│   └── src
│       └── main.rs
└── target
```

There's one `Cargo.lock` and one `target/` at the top, for every member. `cargo new add_one --lib` run in the workspace folder creates a member and adds it to `members` for you.

question.prompt_md: What do the members of a workspace share?

options.text_md: One crate: they all compile into a single library.
Access to each other's code without any declaration.

explanations.text_md: Correct. They're built together, with one set of resolved dependency versions.
Not quite. Each member keeps its own `src/`.
Not quite. Each member is its own package with its own crates.
Not quite. A member uses another only through a declared dependency (next screen).

screens.heading: Depending on a sibling
screens.text_md:
Being in the same workspace doesn't let `adder` use `add_one`. It still has to **depend** on it, here by path: `add_one = { path = "../add_one" }`. Then `adder/src/main.rs` can write `use add_one;` and call `add_one::add_one(num)`, like any other crate.

Without the dependency, `use add_one;` fails with "unresolved import". Workspaces share the build; dependencies stay explicit, which is what keeps each package usable on its own.

code.text:
[package]
name = "adder"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
add_one = { path = "../add_one" }

screens.heading: Choosing a member
screens.text_md:
From the workspace root, `cargo build` builds every member. To run or test one, name it with **`-p`** (package):

- `cargo run -p adder` runs the `adder` program.
- `cargo test -p add_one` runs only `add_one`'s tests.
- `cargo test` runs every member's tests, doc tests included.

panels.title: $ cargo run -p adder
panels.text:
Compiling add_one v0.1.0
   Compiling adder v0.1.0
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s)
     Running `target/debug/adder`
Hello, world! 10 plus one is 11!

question.prompt_md: Fill in the blank to run only the tests of the member `add_one`, from the workspace root.

code.text: cargo test ___ add_one

question.general_md: `-p` (or `--package`) selects one member of the workspace.

wrong_answers.why_md: Cargo has no such flag.
that selects a binary target, and `add_one` is a library.

screens.heading: External dependencies
screens.text_md:
When `add_one` depends on `rand`, the workspace's single `Cargo.lock` records one version of `rand` for every member that uses it, so they stay compatible.

Sharing the lock file doesn't share the dependency: `adder` can't `use rand;` until its own `Cargo.toml` lists `rand` too. Each package says what it uses.

code.text:
[package]
name = "add_one"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"

[dependencies]
rand = "0.8.5"

screens.heading: Tests across the workspace
screens.text_md: Each member keeps its own tests. `cargo test` at the root runs them all: unit tests, integration tests and doc tests of every member, one section per crate. `cargo test -p add_one` narrows it to one member.

panels.title: $ cargo test
panels.text:
running 1 test
test tests::it_works ... ok

test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out

question.prompt_md: In a workspace, `add_one` depends on `rand`. `adder` depends on `add_one` and writes `use rand::Rng;`. What happens?

options.text_md: A compile error: `adder` doesn't list `rand` among its own dependencies.
It works: everything in `Cargo.lock` is available to every member.
It works, because `adder` depends on `add_one`, which depends on `rand`.
Cargo downloads a second copy of `rand` for `adder`.

explanations.text_md: Correct. A package can use only the crates its own `Cargo.toml` names; add `rand` there with the same version.
Not quite. The lock file pins versions; it doesn't grant access.
Not quite. Dependencies of dependencies aren't in scope.
Not quite. Nothing is downloaded for an undeclared dependency; once declared, the shared lock file gives both the same version.

summary: A workspace is a root `Cargo.toml` listing `members`; they share one `Cargo.lock` and one `target/`.
A member uses another through a path dependency: `add_one = { path = "../add_one" }`.
`cargo build` and `cargo test` at the root cover every member; `-p NAME` picks one.
Every package lists its own dependencies; the shared lock file only keeps their versions in step.

lessons.title: `cargo install` and custom commands
lessons.book_section: 14.4 Installing Binaries with `cargo install`; 14.5 Extending Cargo with Custom Commands
lessons.objective_md: Know what `cargo install` does and where it puts programs, and how a program named `cargo-something` becomes a Cargo command.

screens.heading: Installing a program
screens.text_md:
`cargo install` downloads a package from crates.io, builds it with the release profile and copies its **programs** into `~/.cargo/bin`. It's a convenient way for Rust developers to get tools other Rust developers wrote, such as `ripgrep`, a fast `grep` whose program is called `rg`.

It isn't a system package manager: there are no automatic updates, and you install for your own user. This course shows the command; it never runs it.

coming_from.c: Like building a tool from source with `make install`, but into your home folder and from a registry.
coming_from.go: Like `go install example.com/tool@latest`, which puts the binary in `~/go/bin`.
coming_from.java: Like `dotnet tool install --global`. Java has no standard equivalent.
coming_from.js: Like `npm install --global`: it installs a package's command for your user.
coming_from.python: Like `pip install --user` for a command-line tool, or `pipx install`.

panels.title: $ cargo install ripgrep
panels.text:
Updating crates.io index
  Downloaded ripgrep v14.1.1
  Downloaded 1 crate (213.6 KB)
  Installing ripgrep v14.1.1
   Compiling ripgrep v14.1.1
    Finished `release` profile [optimized + debuginfo] target(s)
  Installing ~/.cargo/bin/rg
   Installed package `ripgrep v14.1.1` (executable `rg`)

screens.heading: Programs, not libraries
screens.text_md: Only packages with a **binary** target can be installed: `cargo install` is for programs you run. A library crate is used differently, by listing it under `[dependencies]` in the `Cargo.toml` of the project that needs it. `cargo install rand` fails, because `rand` has no program to install.

question.prompt_md: Where does `cargo install` put the programs it builds?

options.text_md: In the current project's `Cargo.toml`, as a dependency.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Installed programs land in the Cargo home's `bin` folder; with it on your `PATH`, you can run them by name.
Not quite. The build happens in a temporary folder, and the result is copied to `~/.cargo/bin`.
Not quite. `cargo install` installs for your user only.
Not quite. Installing doesn't touch any project's manifest.

screens.heading: `PATH`
screens.text_md: To run an installed program by name, its folder must be in your shell's **`PATH`**, the list of folders the shell searches for commands. `rustup` adds `~/.cargo/bin` when it installs Rust, which is also why `cargo` and `rustc` themselves work. If `rg` isn't found after installing it, `~/.cargo/bin` is missing from `PATH`.

screens.heading: A custom Cargo command
screens.text_md:
When you type `cargo something`, Cargo first checks its own commands, then looks in your `PATH` for a program called **`cargo-something`** and runs it. So a package named `cargo-hello` with this `main`, installed with `cargo install`, becomes `cargo hello`.

Cargo passes the subcommand's own name as the first argument after the program's path, which is why this program shows `"hello"` before the words you typed. `cargo --list` shows every command Cargo can find, built-in and custom.

question.prompt_md: Fill in the blank: an installed program with this name runs as `cargo tidy`.
question.general_md: Cargo looks for a program named `cargo-` followed by the subcommand, anywhere in your `PATH`.

wrong_answers.why_md: Cargo doesn't run arbitrary programs as subcommands, only `cargo-` ones.
the separator is a hyphen.

screens.heading: Read before you install
screens.text_md: `cargo install` builds and runs code written by someone else, with your permissions, and so does a custom subcommand every time you use it. Prefer well-known packages, check the name carefully (look-alike names are a known trick), and read the crate's page and repository first. Building a package can also run its build script, so install only what you'd be willing to run.

problems.comes_after: All chapter lessons and one Medium Accepted
problems.description_md:
Turn Chapter 13's sales analysis into a workspace with a library and a command-line program. The starter has the folders: `core/` holds the library package `analysis-core` with PRJ13's functions (`paid_total`, `product_totals`, `top_products`, `report`), and `cli/` holds an empty program package, `analysis-cli`.

**Part 1 · The workspace**

Make the root `Cargo.toml` a virtual workspace whose members are `core` and `cli`, and make `cli` depend on `analysis-core` by path. `paid_total` in the starter returns 0: restore it (the total value of the paid sales, `quantity × unit_cents` widened to `u128`).

**Part 2 · Documentation**

Document `analysis-core`: a crate-level `//!` comment, and `///` comments with an `# Examples` code example on `product_totals` and on `report`, using `analysis_core::…` paths. `cargo test -p analysis-core --doc` runs them, and `cargo doc` builds.

**Part 3 · The program**

`analysis-cli <file>` reads a sales file. Every line that isn't empty after trimming is `product,quantity,unit_cents,paid`: four comma-separated fields, each trimmed; quantity and unit_cents parse as `u32`; paid is `yes` or `no`. The program prints `report` of the sales, then `Total paid: $D.CC` and a line feed.

Errors go to standard error. Not exactly one argument: `usage: analysis-cli <sales.csv>`, exit code 2. A file that can't be read: `analysis-cli: <file>: <error>`, exit code 1. A bad line: `analysis-cli: line N: expected product,quantity,unit_cents,yes|no` (N counts every line from 1), exit code 1.

**Part 4 · Release**

The workspace builds in release mode, and the program behaves the same; the rows of this part run everything together.

```text
Run:      cargo run -p analysis-cli -- sales.csv     (sales.csv: "tea,2,125,yes\ncake,1,305,yes\ntea,9,999,no\n")
Expected: cake: $3.05

          Total paid: $5.55
```
problems.constraints_md: - Sales files up to 100,000 lines. Integer money only. No `unwrap()`.
hints: Root: `members = ["core", "cli"]`; `cli/Cargo.toml`: `analysis-core = { path = "../core" }`.
A doc example builds a `Vec<Sale>` with `analysis_core::Sale { … }` and checks `report(&sales)` with `assert_eq!`.
In `main`, parse each line with `split(',')` into a `Vec<&str>`, check it has 4 fields, `parse::<u32>()` the numbers and `match` the last field against `"yes"` and `"no"`.
problems.solution_approach_md: The workspace root lists both members; `cli` names `analysis-core` as a path dependency and imports `analysis_core`. `paid_total` is PRJ13's `filter`/`map`/`sum`. The docs follow the standard sections. `main` checks its argument, reads the file, parses each line (numbering every line, skipping blank ones), and prints the report and the formatted total; every failure prints its message and exits with its code.
problems.idiomatic_md: Splitting a program into a library and a thin binary in one workspace keeps the logic testable and documented, while the binary only deals with files, arguments and exit codes.

problems.title: The library as a workspace
problems.description_md:
The library manager is about to grow a second program, so split it the way large Rust projects are split. The starter already has the files in their new places: `core/` holds the library package `library` (every module from LM13, `cli.rs` included), and `app/` holds a binary package `library-app` whose `main.rs` is LM13's. Make it a working, documented workspace.

**Part 1 · The workspace**

The root `Cargo.toml` lists only `core`. Add `app` to the members and give `app/Cargo.toml` a path dependency on the library: `library = { path = "../core" }`. The program then works exactly as in LM13 (`list`, `count`, `find`, `by`, `authors`, `decades`).

**Part 2 · Documentation**

Give `core/src/lib.rs` a crate-level `//!` comment with an `# Examples` section: a code example that makes a `Library`, adds two books with `add_book` and checks with `assert_eq!` what `find` returns. Document `text::sort_key` with `///` and its own `# Examples` example. `cargo test -p library --doc` runs both.

**Part 3 · Profiles**

Debug builds of the library should be a little faster: in the **root** manifest (profiles of members are ignored in a workspace), set `opt-level = 1` for the dev profile. Release builds keep their defaults.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Run:      cargo run -p library-app -- cat.txt authors     (cat.txt: "Emma|Jane Austen|1815\nDune|Frank Herbert|1965\nPersuasion|Jane Austen|1817\n")
Expected: Jane Austen: 2
          Frank Herbert: 1
```
problems.constraints_md:
- The modules' code stays as it is; only manifests and documentation change.
- No `unwrap()`.
hints: Root: `members = ["core", "app"]`, then a `[profile.dev]` table with `opt-level = 1`.
A crate-level doc example: `//! use library::Library;` then `//! let mut lib = Library::new();` and so on, all inside a fence that starts with `//! ```` .
`sort_key("The Hobbit")` is `"Hobbit"`; an example can show that and a title without an article.
problems.solution_approach_md: Listing `app` as a member and giving it the path dependency makes `use library::cli::{Config, run};` in `main.rs` resolve again. The crate-level `//!` documentation shows the library's main use in a runnable example, and `sort_key`'s `///` example shows its contract. `[profile.dev]` in the root manifest applies to every member.
problems.idiomatic_md: In a workspace, profiles live in the root manifest only; Cargo warns about (and ignores) a `[profile]` in a member. Settings that depend on the package, such as dependencies, stay in the member manifests.
problems.source_checks_md: - Part 2: a crate-level `//!` comment with an `# Examples` code example; `///` docs with `# Examples` on `sort_key`. Banned: `unwrap()`.
problems.notes_md: The supplied files are the LM13 reference package in workspace folders, so every learner starts from the same code. The starter builds only the library; the program package isn't a member yet. Each part is graded on its own submission.
